column13: Roman and more recent (Mamluk?) architectural features, many deep cisterns, some bedrock mortars. The top of the site has a lot of exposed bedrock. A partly collapsed Mamluk (?) building at the northeast corner of the site, with the two collapsed arches that once supported the roof clearly visible. The high densities of pottery are actually on the slopes around the highest part of the hill, since it is mostly cleared down to bedrock on the top.This site was reported by Nelson Glueck (1951: 185), who only appears to have visited the top of the hill, where he found mostly Roman and later pottery and only a small number of worn sherds that might be Iron Age or MB II. Early Bronze, Middle/Late Bronze, and Iron Age pottery is frequent on the slopes and terraces SW of the citadel (site element 203).

A rather large Early Bronze site, with fairly dense scatter of pottery, much lower density of lithics and ground stone. A stone stairway about 10 m west of two caves with bedrock mortars above them (waypoint 2262). Large cairns of stones scattered about the upper parts of the hill as well as the modern terrace walls probably derive from EB architecture that was once here, but stratified remains may still exist. The lowest parts of the scatter, in a vegetable field below and north of the olive grove (polygon xxx), may derive from the upper part of the site. Quite a few sickle elements. Pottery very similar to finds at Glueck’s Ras Abû Lôfah, and both Glueck and MEGA-Jordan appear to have located this site in the wrong place on maps. A local farmer confirmed that this is the correct Râs Abu Lôfeh
